## Conversational walkthrough — ray_molformer dftracer pipeline

This session set out to annotate, trace, and optimize IBM MoLFormer (a chemical-language transformer) running distributed via Ray Train on Tuolumne's AMD MI300A GPUs. What made this session unusual was how much of the effort went into getting a single real, traced, multi-node training run to work at all — the optimization work itself, once the infrastructure was solid, was comparatively fast.

**Getting STEP 7 (the baseline traced run) working took resolving a long chain of root causes**, each one only visible after the previous was fixed: a silent dftracer ABI mismatch that made "successful" builds produce zero trace data; a ROCm/jemalloc static-TLS collision that killed Ray's GCS server with a misleading 35-second timeout instead of an obvious crash; a Spindle library-loader deadlock that only showed up after many rapid debugging restarts; a Ray worker-registration storm caused by an unset `--num-cpus` flag defaulting to the full 192-core hardware count; environment-variable scoping bugs where fixes applied to the driver process silently didn't reach Ray's forked worker processes; and finally a genuinely subtle dftracer tracing gap where the actual dataset-reading task process never flushed its trace buffer before teardown, fixed with a targeted patch to Ray Data's own `csv_datasource.py`.

Each of these was root-caused with direct evidence — `strace`, reading Ray's own installed source code, `/proc` process inspection — rather than guessed at, because several plausible-sounding first guesses turned out to be wrong once checked (a "the stats file must be from a different dataset" hypothesis for the NaN bug, a "the CSV must be re-read every epoch" hypothesis for a metadata-op-count anomaly, an assumption that Ray Train enables `find_unused_parameters` by default) — all three were disproven by directly reading source or resolving trace file-hash records to real paths.

Once a real baseline run was in hand, the diagnosis was clean: this workload is compute-bound at the trace-layer level, though a deeper investigation later in the session revealed that most of the actual *wall-clock* time is Ray Train's own worker startup, not the training loop itself — an important distinction that reframes where future optimization effort should go.

The optimization pass itself was honest rather than favorable: bf16 mixed precision, the obvious and correctly-prioritized first thing to try, measured as flat-to-slightly-slower rather than faster, and 4-node scaling measured as slower than 2-node — both reported as genuine negative findings. Along the way, a real correctness bug (NaN training loss from RDKit descriptor edge cases) was found and fixed. The communication dimension surfaced the most promising *unmeasured* lever for next time: RCCL likely defaulting to the slow management network interface instead of the fast Slingshot fabric, discovered through direct network-interface probing rather than trace analysis.

The session closed by fixing several of its own tools rather than just working around them: `session_final_report` now generates a PDF automatically, checks REPORT.md's structural completeness, anonymizes patch files, and runs a README reproducibility smoke test — all deterministically, every call, instead of relying on an agent to remember and improvise each of these separately each session.
